title: Five centimetres taller on average
hook: Two seed batches differ a little on average. What about the tallest plants?

knows: values spread around them in a bell shape (averages-turn-bell-shaped)
doesNotKnow: that a small difference in averages becomes a large ratio far out in the tails

misconception: If two groups' averages differ only a little, the very high values will come from both groups about equally.
objective: The learner can say that with equal spreads (10 cm) a 5 cm gap in averages makes batch B 82% of the plants above 130 cm and 88% above 140 cm, because A's curve falls away faster in the tail.

claims.text: For two normal distributions with sd 10 cm and means 100 cm (A) and 105 cm (B), the share above 130 cm is 0.135% and 0.621% (135 and 621 per 100,000); B makes up 82% of plants above 130 cm, about 4.6 to 1.
claims.source: Q(3) = 0.00135, Q(2.5) = 0.00621 (standard normal table); model.ts tailA/tailB/shareB/ratio (erfc, Numerical Recipes erfcc) in node 2026-10-14: 0.1350%, 0.6210%, 82.14%, 4.600. Seeded cross-check (brief): mulberry32(11), 100,000 per batch: A 122, B 667.

claims.text: Above 140 cm the shares are 0.0032% and 0.0233% (3 and 23 per 100,000); B makes up 88%, about 7.3 to 1, so the ratio keeps growing further out.
At the averages the two batches overlap almost completely: B is only 5 cm (half a spread) taller.
claims.source: Means 100 and 105 with sd 10: the curves' peaks are 0.5 sd apart; overlap coefficient 2*Phi(-0.25) = 0.80 (node). The picture draws both curves.

claims.text: The batches are a model with equal spreads, equal sizes and exact bell shapes; 'spread (10 cm)' in the question is the standard deviation. Real data with different spreads or shapes can give different tail ratios.
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief Round 3 item 4, planned claim 3); the curves are drawn exactly (model.ts density), no sampling. Plants only; no human-group example in learner text (brief's content boundary).

recall.question: Two groups have the same spread, and group B's average is a little higher. Among the very highest values, what do you expect?
options: B is heavily over-represented, more so the further out you go
B is over-represented by the same small margin at every height
recall.why: With equal spreads, the lower group's bell curve falls away faster in the tail, so the ratio of B to A grows the further out the cutoff is.
